questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Define the risk difference and state what it measures.
questions.stem: A translator's note records that 6 per cent of readers of the localised welcome email unsubscribed, while 9 per cent of readers of the original did. What does the risk difference give the team?

options.text: A direct comparison of the two event rates, which here is a gap of 3 percentage points.
A conversion of both rates into odds, which removes the need to report the raw rates.
options.misconception: Replaces the rate comparison with an odds ratio

options.text: A ratio of one rate to the other, which here would be 1.5 for the localised version.
options.misconception: Reports a ratio where a difference is needed

options.text: A comparison of the two sample sizes, which shows whether the groups were balanced.
options.misconception: Compares sample sizes rather than event rates

questions.explanation: A risk difference subtracts one event rate from the other, so 9 per cent minus 6 per cent is 3 percentage points. Ratios, odds and sample-size comparisons answer different questions.
questions.hint: Subtract one event rate from the other.

options.misconception: Believes pairing means two raters per passage

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Standardised mean difference from a test statistic
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a standardised mean difference is recovered from a t-statistic.
questions.stem: A translator's note records a t-statistic of 2.0 for two groups of 25 passages each, and explains in writing how the standardised mean difference follows from it.

answer.exemplar: The standardised mean difference multiplies the t-statistic by the square root of the combined sample size divided by the product of the two group sizes. With 25 passages in each group that factor is the square root of 50 over 625, so multiplying 2.0 by about 0.283 gives a standardised difference of roughly 0.57, which places the two groups about half a spread apart.

questions.explanation: The standardised difference is the t-statistic multiplied by the square root of one over n1 plus one over n2, so a t of 2.0 with 25 per group gives about 0.57. The raw t hides the size of the gap.
questions.hint: Multiply t by the standard error factor.

options.misconception: Chooses the threshold after seeing the effect size

options.text: Compare the p-value with the threshold, then treat the outcome as practically important at once.
options.misconception: Treats statistical significance as practical importance

options.text: Read the sample size, then use it to work out the p-value the data must beat.
options.misconception: Believes the sample size determines the p-value

questions.explanation: A p-value is compared with the threshold that applies, and the effect size shows whether the difference matters. Choosing a threshold after seeing results, or reading significance as importance, misuses the statistic.
questions.hint: Compare first, then judge the size.

options.misconception: Believes a small sample changes the critical value

options.misconception: Explains width by rounding rather than by the standard error

questions.explanation: Both methods share the same spread and confidence level, so only the standard error differs, and ten times more tickets make it smaller. A smaller standard error gives a narrower interval.

options.misconception: Believes a p-value settles practical importance

options.text: It shows how many readers improved, and the p-value shows how that count was reached.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the choice of denominator changes a retention rate.
questions.stem: A translator's note explains in writing why it reports retention against the original number of readers rather than against the number who finished the first lesson.

answer.exemplar: Retention answers whether people came back, and the denominator decides what that question means. Measured against the original readers it captures both the people who never started and the ones who stopped early, so it reflects the whole funnel. Measured against finishers it flatters the material by ignoring the readers who left before the first session ended.

questions.explanation: Dividing by the original count includes readers who never started, so the rate reflects the whole funnel. Dividing by finishers inflates the figure by ignoring the readers who dropped out early.
questions.hint: The denominator changes what is measured.

options.misconception: Treats a p-value near the threshold as though it passed

options.text: The width is 1.8, and more observations at the same spread would narrow it.
The width is 1.8, and raising the confidence level would narrow it.
options.misconception: Believes a higher confidence level narrows the interval

options.text: The width is 5.0, and rounding the limits to whole numbers would narrow it.

options.text: The width is 0.9, and repeating the same measurements would narrow it.
options.misconception: Halves the width by mistake and repeats data

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a paired design is preferred to two independent groups.
questions.stem: A translator's note explains in writing why a paired comparison of translations is preferred to comparing two separate groups of readers.

answer.exemplar: A paired design compares each passage with itself before and after editing, so passages that are simply harder to write cancel out of the comparison. Only the change produced by the editing remains to be measured, and the analysis is based on the differences rather than on two noisy sets of independent scores. Separate groups would mix the editing effect with the natural differences between passages.

questions.explanation: Pairing removes the effect of passages that are simply harder, so the measured difference reflects editing itself. Two separate groups mix the editing effect with the natural differences between passages.
questions.hint: Say what cancels out in a paired design.

answer.exemplar: The test result says whether a difference could have arisen by chance, which depends as much on the sample size as on the difference itself. questions.stem: A translator's note asks the team to define the risk difference in a way that survives translation into other locales.

options.text: The difference between two event rates, expressed in the same units as the rates themselves.
The difference between two event rates, expressed as a percentage of the smaller rate.
options.misconception: Defines it as a relative percentage of the baseline

options.text: The ratio of two event rates, expressed as a number greater than one.
options.misconception: Defines the risk difference as a ratio

options.text: The number of events in one group minus the number of events in the other group.
options.misconception: Defines it on raw counts rather than rates

questions.explanation: A risk difference is a subtraction of two rates, reported in the same units as the rates, which keeps it interpretable across locales. Ratios depend on a baseline and raw counts depend on group sizes.
questions.hint: Same units as the rates.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Report the direction of paired changes without hiding reversals.
questions.stem: A translator's note holds paired ratings of 20 passages, where 12 passages improved, 5 worsened and 3 stayed the same. What does the note support?

options.text: That more passages improved than worsened, and that a minority moved the other way.
That 60 per cent of passages improved, which is the strongest claim the data allow.
options.misconception: Reports a proportion and hides the passages that worsened

options.text: That every passage either improved or worsened, since only 3 stayed the same.
options.misconception: Treats a small number of unchanged passages as none

options.text: That the change was harmful overall, since 5 passages worsened at all.
options.misconception: Judges the overall effect by the worst cases

questions.explanation: The note can say that 12 passages improved against 5 that worsened, so the direction favours the change while a minority moved against it. Quoting only the improved proportion would hide the reversals.
questions.hint: Report both directions of the change.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Compute a later retention rate against the original cohort.
questions.stem: A translator's note records that 45 of the 60 readers of a translated guide returned after 30 days, and 30 of those 45 returned again after 90 days. What is the 90-day retention rate as a percentage of the original 60 readers?
questions.explanation: Thirty of the original 60 readers is one half, so the 90-day retention rate is 50 per cent. Measured against the 45 who returned at 30 days it would be 67 per cent, which flatters the guide.
questions.hint: Divide by the original number of readers.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Standardised mean difference from a test statistic
questions.learningObjective: Explain the reconstruction of a standardised mean difference from a t-statistic.
questions.stem: A translator's note explains in writing how a standardised mean difference can be recovered from a reported t-statistic.

answer.exemplar: The t-statistic divides the difference between the group means by the standard error of that difference. Multiplying it by the square root of one over n1 plus one over n2 converts that error into the pooled spread, giving a standardised difference expressed in units of the spread rather than in the original measurement. The note can then compare it with effects reported from other locale studies.

questions.explanation: Because the t-statistic expresses the gap in units of its standard error, multiplying by the square root of one over n1 plus one over n2 converts it into pooled spread units. The result is comparable across studies.
questions.hint: Rescale the t by the error factor.
